question: For a conventional (non-PWC) vessel towing a skier in Texas, during what specific window is towing illegal, more precisely than simply 'sunset to sunrise'?
choice_a: From one-half hour after sunset until one-half hour before sunrise
choice_b: From exactly sunset until exactly sunrise, with no buffer
choice_c: From one hour after sunset until one hour before sunrise
choice_d: Towing is illegal only after midnight
explanation: Texas boater education material specifies that operators of conventional boats towing a person on water skis, skiboards, or similar devices may not do so between one-half hour after sunset and one-half hour before sunrise; personal watercraft face a stricter sunset-to-sunrise rule.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- towing hours for conventional vessels

question: If a PWC operator tows a skier without using an onboard observer (relying on a mirror instead), what is the minimum passenger rating the PWC must have?
choice_b: At least two -- the operator and the retrieved skier
choice_c: No minimum rating applies without an observer
choice_d: At least three, the same as when an observer is used
explanation: When towing without an observer aboard, a PWC must still be rated to carry at least two people -- the operator and the skier once retrieved from the water; using an observer raises that minimum to three (operator, observer, skier).
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- PWC towing capacity without an observer

question: Why do most personal watercraft (PWC) operators in Texas use an observer rather than a mirror when towing a skier?
choice_a: Because Texas law bans mirrors on PWCs entirely
choice_b: Because PWCs are not permitted to tow skiers under any circumstance
choice_c: Because most PWC mirrors do not meet the size and view standards Texas law requires for towing
choice_d: Because observers cost less to install than mirrors
explanation: Texas boater education material notes that most PWC mirrors are too small or improperly positioned to meet the legal size and viewing standards, so PWC operators towing a skier typically rely on an observer instead.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- PWC mirror limitations

question: Besides meeting the minimum four-inch size standard, what additional requirement must a towing vessel's rearview mirror satisfy under Texas law?
choice_a: It must be tinted to reduce glare
choice_b: It must be replaced every boating season
choice_c: It must be certified by the U.S. Coast Guard as a navigation device
choice_d: It must be mounted so the operator has a full, complete view beyond the rear of the vessel at all times
explanation: Beyond the four-inch minimum dimensions, the mirror used in place of an observer must be mounted so it gives the operator a full, complete view to the rear of the vessel at all times, not just meet a size threshold.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- mirror mounting/view requirement

question: Under Texas law, which specific act toward another vessel or swimmer is expressly prohibited for an operator towing a skier?
choice_a: Buzzing or spraying another vessel or swimmer
choice_b: Waving to another vessel while towing
choice_d: Displaying a ski flag near another vessel
explanation: Texas boating rules expressly make it illegal to buzz or spray another vessel or swimmer, a form of careless or reckless operation that towing operators must avoid.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- prohibited conduct while towing

question: Under Texas law, when is a vessel operator permitted to drive in a circular course around a person in the water?
choice_a: At any time, as circling a swimmer is never restricted
choice_b: Only when retrieving a downed water-skier or person engaged in a similar towed activity
choice_c: Only if the person in the water signals with both arms raised
explanation: Texas law generally restricts operating a vessel in a circular course around a person in the water, but makes an exception for an operator who is retrieving a downed skier or similar towed participant.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- circular-course exception for retrieving a downed skier

question: What is required of the personal flotation device (PFD) a water skier wears in Texas, beyond simply being USCG-approved?
choice_b: It must match the color of the tow boat
choice_c: It must also be designed for water-skiing use -- a ski belt alone does not meet the USCG-approved requirement
choice_d: No PFD is required if the skier is an experienced swimmer
explanation: A water skier's PFD must be both USCG-approved and designed for water-skiing; a ski belt by itself is not considered a USCG-approved PFD and does not satisfy the requirement.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- PFD design requirement for skiers

question: What types of USCG-approved PFD satisfy the requirement for a person riding on or being towed behind a PWC in Texas?
choice_b: Any flotation device, including pool noodles
choice_c: Only Type I offshore life jackets
choice_d: Type I, II, III, or V
explanation: Texas law requires each person riding on or being towed behind a PWC to wear a USCG-approved Type I, II, III, or V personal flotation device.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- PFD types for PWC riders/towed persons

question: While towing a skier, how far should the operator keep the skier from shoreline, docks, hazards, and people in the water, according to Texas boater education guidance?
choice_a: At least twice the length of the tow rope
choice_b: Exactly the length of the tow rope
choice_d: Half the length of the tow rope
explanation: Texas boater education guidance directs operators to keep a towed skier at a safe distance of at least twice the length of the tow rope away from the shoreline, docks, hazards, and people in the water.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- towing safe-distance guidance

question: Before a fallen skier is allowed to approach and board the tow boat, what must the operator do?
choice_a: Increase engine speed to hold position
choice_b: Shut off the engine to prevent propeller injuries
choice_d: Release the tow rope into the water
explanation: To avoid propeller injuries, the operator must shut off the engine before allowing a skier to approach and board the boat.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- engine safety before skier boards

question: Before starting the engine to begin towing a skier, what must the operator first confirm?
choice_a: That the skier has removed their PFD
choice_b: That another vessel is within 50 feet
choice_c: That no one in the water is near the propeller
choice_d: That the fuel tank is completely full
explanation: An operator must confirm no one in the water is near the propeller before starting the engine to begin a tow, preventing propeller-strike injuries at the start of the activity.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- starting the engine safely before towing

question: If a boat is towing more than one skier at the same time in Texas, what is required of the tow lines?
choice_a: Each tow line must be a different length to avoid collisions
choice_b: Only one tow line may be used regardless of the number of skiers
choice_c: Tow line length is not a safety consideration
choice_d: The tow lines must be of the same length
explanation: When towing multiple skiers simultaneously, the tow lines must be the same length so the skiers stay level with each other, reducing the risk of the lines crossing or the skiers colliding.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- multiple-skier tow line length

question: Do Texas towing regulations that apply to water skiing, such as hours of operation, also apply to wake surfing behind a boat?
choice_a: Yes -- a wake surfer must comply with all regulations applicable to water skiers, including the time and manner of operation
choice_b: No, wake surfing is entirely unregulated in Texas
choice_c: No, wake surfing is only regulated on federal waterways
choice_d: Only the observer requirement applies to wake surfing, not the hours restriction
explanation: Texas boater education material specifies that a wake surfer must comply with all regulations that apply to water skis or other aquaplanes, including the time and manner of operation, such as the sunset-to-sunrise restriction.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- wake surfing regulatory parity with water skiing

question: Because wake surfing boats intentionally generate a large wake, what must the operator do regarding nearby structures and vessels?
choice_a: Operate as close as possible to shore to keep the wake contained
choice_b: Maintain distance from shorelines, docks, navigation aids, and other vessels to avoid creating a hazardous wake or wash
choice_c: Disable the boat's ballast system near any dock
choice_d: No distance precautions are needed since the wake dissipates instantly
explanation: Because a wake surfing boat intentionally produces a larger wake, the operator must keep a safe distance from shorelines, marine structures, navigation aids, and other vessels to avoid creating a hazardous wake or wash.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- wake surfing distance from structures/vessels

question: After falling or dropping the tow rope, what should a skier do with their ski or other device?
choice_a: Let it float away to avoid extra weight
choice_b: Submerge it to mark the location for divers
choice_c: Hold it up out of the water so the boat operator and other vessels can see the skier's location
choice_d: Attach it to the tow rope and release both
explanation: A fallen skier should hold a ski or similar device up out of the water so the boat operator and nearby vessels can see them, improving visibility until pickup.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- skier visibility after falling

question: Why should a water skier never wrap any part of the tow rope around their body?
choice_a: Because it voids the boat's warranty
choice_b: Because it interferes with the boat's GPS
choice_c: There is no safety concern; it is simply discouraged by tradition
choice_d: Because doing so risks the skier being dragged or entangled if they fall or the line goes taut unexpectedly
explanation: Wrapping the tow rope around the body creates a serious entanglement and dragging hazard if the skier falls or the line suddenly pulls taut, which is why skiers are taught never to do this.
source_note: TPWD-approved Texas boater education course -- tow rope entanglement hazard
